body:
Updated: I also tested another approach. I built a Windows version on Linux and ran it with the flag `wine ./game.exe --rendering-driver d3d12`, and I see that the errors do not occur there. That is, D3D12 handles texels correctly and properly sends commands to Vulkan.

Tomorrow I will check on several Windows machines with Nvidia cards to see if such errors appear on other GPUs, also using the `--rendering-driver d3d12` flag to get a more precise understanding. Overall, though, I think DirectX handles texels the same way as Vulkan.
This looks like an NVidia driver bug. In OpenGL the code you write in a shader goes directly to the OpenGL driver to be compiled. We don't touch it at all.

> It's also possible that your shader has a calculation error, such as a division by zero error, out-of-bounds memory access, or other illegal operations. Each graphics card handles these exceptions differently; some may skip them entirely, while others may cause the entire model to fail to render. You can use NVIDIA's debugging tools to check what the problem is. The probability of such a problem occurring in a basic function is very low.

Yes, I think this is somehow related to how Nvidia or OpenGL 3 limit texels. I’ll try to check this on other Nvidia graphics cards.

> This looks like an NVidia driver bug. In OpenGL the code you write in a shader goes directly to the OpenGL driver to be compiled. We don't touch it at all.

Then if OpenGL 3 works without any changes, that is very strange. But you are right that Nvidia looks like a driver bug; the problem is that they were using the latest drivers. I will also try to check this on several Nvidia graphics cards. But in theory OpenGL 3 should not have produced such an error in any case.

> Then if OpenGL 3 works without any changes, that is very strange. But you are right that Nvidia looks like a driver bug; the problem is that they were using the latest drivers. I will also try to check this on several Nvidia graphics cards. But in theory OpenGL 3 should not have produced such an error in any case.

NVidia doesn't invest a lot in the OpenGL drivers these days. Its not surprising that the OpenGL shader compiler has a bug when the Vulkan/D3D12 drivers don't.

Hello again. I tested the setup on 4 machines: - 3060 and 3070 (photos were above, it doesn’t work on Nvidia/DirectX) - GeForce GTX 1650 SUPER (Nvidia) (DirectX) - GeForce GTX 1070 (Nvidia) (DirectX) I remind you — all the test machines had the latest drivers. Also, we had 2 more or less modern machines and 2 older ones. Now we can definitely say that the problem is in Godot or the shader. But the thing is, there’s nothing wrong in the shader except for the texelFetch operation. Also, in other engines, there are no such problems if you run a game on these machines, which again points to an issue specifically in Godot. I also tested this on the new v4.7.dev1.official [bf95b6258]. So I don’t think @clayjohn was right, although I agree with him in part. I agree more with @zhangjiangen11 — it really seemed to me that the issue is precisely in how texelFetch handles the data. And yes, I thought it would be a good idea to drop a build, but there’s nothing in it except the menu, so yes, you can try to debug this or see how it behaves on Nvidia/DirectX. Build (if anything, the archive contains the files directly, not in a folder): https://github.com/miruji/CaveVox-260218-x86_64-windows-debug

Again, Godot doesn't do anything to your shader. The shader code is sent directly to the GPU driver's shader compiler. So the problem is with the shader or with the GPU driver. There is nothing we can do in Godot to improve this

> You’re wrong to say that you can’t do anything – you just don’t want to. If you wanted, you would at least test the minimal build.

You are right. I am not willing to debug your shader code for you. This is a space for reporting bugs with Godot. This isn't a Godot bug, so I am not willing to help you any further
